title: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
desc: Balances independent reasoning and supervised AI practice while rejecting both inevitable cognitive harm and unrestricted assistance.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns how to combine independent legal reasoning with AI competence, not simply whether law schools should embrace or reject AI.
kps.d: Berkeley, Chicago and Texas identify independent judgment as essential to responsible AI use. Critics of broad restrictions also accept the need for unaided learning, but argue that supervising AI constitutes a skill students must practise. The disagreement concerns the timing, breadth and default status of permissions: protected foundational work and specialist AI courses versus integration across ordinary coursework. These positions express educational objectives and professional forecasts, not demonstrated superiority of one curriculum.

qs.q: But the current state of the technology requires that AI use be coupled with the cognitive skills necessary to strategically deploy the technology, to critically assess its work product, and to uphold ethical obligations to clients and to the legal system.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Policy, UC Berkeley School of Law (effective Summer 2026) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: The feedback we have received throughout this process has been consistent: We need to ensure that our students actually learn to think critically, strategically, and independently without relying on AI; but we also must face the reality that AI tools are already widely available to our students, and our graduates will be expected to be prepared to use them in legal practice.
qs.a: Rethinking Legal Education in the AI Era (AI Strategy Statement) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Berkeley exemplifies a broad restrictive default, but neither its policy nor the wider institutional landscape amounts to a uniform ban on AI learning.
kps.d: Effective Summer 2026, Berkeley prohibits AI assistance from conceptualisation through editing and translation of credit-bearing work, restricts exam use, and bars course-material uploads. Paper research may use AI only to identify sources. Instructors can authorise departures with written notice and disclosure. Perlman’s archive documents materially different boundaries elsewhere, including permission for private study, brainstorming or grammar assistance. Ambrogi’s August 2, 2026 analysis finds permission-based defaults common among catalogued schools and qualifies his earlier portrayal of Berkeley as exceptional, while retaining his criticism of its breadth.

qs.q: Rule: The use of AI is prohibited for aid in conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Policy, UC Berkeley School of Law (effective Summer 2026) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: What schools are doing:** The catalogued approaches generally allow limited non-submitted study support while preserving independent judgment and accuracy checks.
qs.a: AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Evidence of stronger AI-assisted work does not establish durable learning gains or inevitable cognitive decline.
kps.d: Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence reports faster work and disproportionate quality gains for less-skilled students, while treating dependence and compressed grades as risks or predictions. Perlman cites a randomised study of 137 upper-level students with quality gains on at least four of six tasks. More directly relevant to learning, a reported 2026 experiment with 91 Minnesota students found no reduction in subsequent unaided performance after initial AI assistance; AI revision improved weaker drafts but worsened stronger ones. Vals AI benchmarking and an unpublished Stanford-led comparison of professors’ preferences assess output performance, not student learning. These findings support task- and stage-specific inquiry rather than a general conclusion about educational effects.

qs.q: legal work product significantly more quickly (a skill that is typ-                        ically rewarded on timed law school exams), but also that it can                        disproportionately improve the quality of that work product for                        less-skilled students.
qs.a: Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Advocates of integration frame supervised AI practice as preparation for client responsibility, but the claimed harms of restrictive education remain prospective.
kps.d: Ambrogi, Tobin and Irwin, and Closing the AI Readiness Gap argue that students should learn to identify fabricated authorities, challenge reasoning and correct drafts before relying on AI in client matters. The readiness framework reports 77% encountering AI in pre-graduation legal work, without supplying survey methods in the excerpt. The Law Student Pulse report describes uneven preparation, employer training and concealed student use. Court sanctions establish that unchecked AI output can have professional consequences; they do not establish that school restrictions cause those consequences. Student testimony and recruitment anecdotes likewise illustrate concerns without measuring the causal effects of bans.

qs.q: That is not just the ability to use AI, but also to supervise it – to spot the hallucinated citation, to recognize when an AI outline has buried the strongest argument, to feel where a generated draft is confidently wrong.
qs.a: In Banning AI, Is Berkeley Law Shortchanging Its Students -- and Endangering their Future Clients? · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: Seventy-seven percent of law students encounter gen AI in their legal work before they graduate.
qs.a: Closing the AI Readiness Gap: A Framework for Law Schools · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Staged instruction offers a practical alternative to both unrestricted assistance and blanket prohibition.
kps.d: Chicago’s 2026–27 pilots pair protected first-year core learning with unaided writing followed by supervised AI-assisted research, revision and drafting iterations. Bliss proposes critique exercises, tutors, simulations and stage-specific permissions; Ambrogi recommends correcting deliberately flawed AI briefs. Reported Washington University instruction combines traditional research foundations with checking generated results. Suffolk proposes differentiated rules and a curriculum review rather than a permanent settlement. These initiatives aim to teach both independent competence and verification; course descriptions, consultation and student satisfaction do not yet demonstrate that they achieve those aims.

qs.q: Our approach will treat writing *without *AI as the foundation and will layer writing *with *AI onto it.
qs.a: Rethinking Legal Education in the AI Era (AI Strategy Statement) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: This in- cludes detailed examples of exercises where students learn to collaborate with generative AI, evaluate AI-produced research and writing, create their own AI tutors and debate partners, role-play with chatbots in classroom simulations, and reflect on the responsible use of generative AI in the legal profession.
qs.a: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Assessment reform seeks observable student understanding, but tighter control can sacrifice valuable forms of sustained writing.
kps.d: Hill reports professors using oral finals, handwritten exams and locked-down tests while still incorporating AI into teaching. Chicago pilots no-access core examinations, and Suffolk proposes secure foundational assessments alongside staged submissions, process records and oral defences. Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence argues that prohibitions need technological controls or proctoring rather than honour codes alone. The countervailing concern is educational: Chicago warns that replacing substantial papers with supervised classroom writing loses extended independent effort, while Perlman rejects treating all unproctored work as invalid. These are practices and rationales, not measured reductions in misconduct or improvements in learning.

qs.q: In his smaller classes, such as Data Privacy & Security Law, he’s brought back a tried-and-true method to make sure his students know the material and are not relying too heavily on AI: one-on-one, 30-minute oral exams.
qs.a: Some law profs move to old-school assessment methods to combat AI · Market & press · 2026

kps.k: Implementation requires separate rules for permission, disclosure, accuracy, privacy and fair enforcement.
kps.d: Permission to use AI does not remove students’ responsibility for citations or substantive work, and disclosure does not itself authorise otherwise prohibited assistance. Embedded features in ordinary writing and research tools complicate definitions and enforcement. Perlman warns that AI detectors cannot alone establish misconduct; Berkeley treats nonexistent citations as a presumption, not automatic proof, of prohibited use. Upload restrictions separately protect course content, confidentiality and student contributions. Equity arguments cut both ways: Bliss and Perlman warn that unequal tool access may justify limits, while Tobin and Irwin argue that banning grammar assistance can penalise learning differences. Faculty AI-assisted feedback also requires transparency and retained human responsibility under Suffolk’s proposals.

qs.q: Students are responsible for the accuracy of their research and all other aspects of their submitted work.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence Policy, UC Berkeley School of Law (effective Summer 2026) · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Even if the policy is limited to “generative AI,” generative AI features are now available in or alongside many commonly used tools, including Grammarly, Microsoft Word, Westlaw products, and Lexis+ (although availability depends on the product and license).
qs.a: Recommended Next Steps on Artificial Intelligence and Teaching (memorandum to Suffolk Law faculty) · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Policy inventories establish varied institutional responses, not which approach works; rapid technological change strengthens the case for review.
kps.d: Ambrogi’s analysis of a 128-school archive snapshot and the supplied 163-school archive version describe different coverage and should not be combined into an adoption trend. Topic counts concern catalogued records, omissions do not prove absent policies, and the AI-assisted archive was not wholly independently verified. The ABA Task Force’s course and practical-training percentages concern responding schools only. Across these materials, restrictions coexist with expanding instruction, but pilots, proposals and future requirements must remain distinct from operative rules. Chicago prioritises adaptable judgment over current tools and commits to revision; Suffolk’s proposed interim safeguards expire June 30, 2027 unless extended or replaced.

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition’s middle path and materially develop it into curricular, assessment and governance models. Their common rationale is that legal education must preserve independent reasoning and writing while also teaching students to supervise, verify and critically evaluate AI output before professional reliance. Several sources translate that balance into staged instruction: protected foundational or unaided work, followed by supervised AI-assisted research, drafting or revision, with course-specific permissions and observable assessment of student understanding. Research-oriented contributions further qualify the proposition by distinguishing improved AI-assisted work product from durable learning gains and by treating cognitive decline as a contingent risk rather than an established consequence. They also add implementation concerns involving verification, disclosure, privacy, accessibility, equitable access, unreliable detection and periodic policy review. Material variation concerns defaults and timing rather than the underlying dual objective: Chicago, Suffolk, Bliss, Tobin and Irwin favour broad or staged integration; other sources endorse the balance without specifying sequencing; Berkeley redirects it toward broad default restrictions on assessed work with instructor-authorised exceptions. The policy archive is descriptive rather than prescriptive and does not establish which model works. These curated sources therefore build on the proposition overall, but should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally, and their pilots, forecasts and policy rationales are not evidence of comparative educational effectiveness.

qs.q: Our approach will treat writing *without *AI as the foundation and will layer writing *with *AI onto it.
qs.a: Rethinking Legal Education in the AI Era (AI Strategy Statement) · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: The selected market-analyst, consultancy and press sources broadly accept the proposition that legal education should protect independent reasoning while providing supervised, critical AI practice. They materially develop it through concrete implementation models: correcting flawed AI briefs, combining foundational research with verification of generated results, allowing AI only at specified writing stages, and using oral, handwritten or locked-down assessments to establish unaided competence. Material variation concerns the breadth of restrictions. Ambrogi criticises Berkeley’s three-year default as overbroad and potentially delaying supervisory practice, while other reporting identifies instructor-controlled restrictions on assessed work as compatible with purposeful AI instruction elsewhere. One source addresses uneven adoption and curricular obsolescence without taking a position on staged instruction. Across the curated sources, the case rests mainly on policy descriptions, educator testimony and prospective practice-readiness concerns, not measured evidence that these approaches improve learning; their selection and number do not establish prevalence among analysts, consultancies or the press generally.

qs.q: An assignment that asks a student to critique and correct a deliberately flawed AI-generated brief simultaneously tests judgment and builds AI competency.
qs.a: In Banning AI, Is Berkeley Law Shortchanging Its Students -- and Endangering their Future Clients? · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: WashU Law is integrating AI as a tool to be used critically and effectively, not as a replacement for human legal reasoning.
qs.a: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The selected legal-tech vendor source supports the proposition’s core balance: students should retain independent understanding and judgment while receiving responsible AI-use instruction, rather than face blanket prohibitions. Its principal reasons are that bans may conceal rather than prevent use, inconsistent preparation may shift training burdens to employers, and students need both AI competence and the ability to assess and apply material independently. The source’s emphasis differs somewhat from the synthesis: it is more directly critical of broad bans and favourable to integration, but it neither endorses unrestricted assistance nor provides a concrete staged curriculum. Its claims about underground use, recruitment and employer burdens are based partly on student testimony and anecdotes rather than demonstrated causal effects. Because this facet contains one curated source, these findings describe that source’s position and do not establish the prevalence of this view among legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: So, instead of focusing so much on whether                                 students are using AI, the conversation should be more about whether they                                 actually understand the material and can apply it on their own.
qs.a: 2026 Law Student Pulse Survey: How Law Students Understand AI Better than Their Institutions · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition’s central middle path and materially develop it into an educational programme: preserve independent legal reasoning and accountable authorship while teaching supervised, critical AI use. Their common reasons are that generative AI can improve speed and work-product quality, particularly for less-skilled students, and is becoming relevant to practice, yet its outputs require verification, substantive editing and retained human understanding. They also share doubts about blanket bans because unreliable detection can produce false accusations or reward undetected noncompliance. Material variation concerns sequencing and enforcement. Lawyering in the Age of Artificial Intelligence most directly favours selective restrictions in some classes followed by explicit upper-level training, closely anticipating the staged proposition. Generative Artificial Intelligence and the Practice of Law places greater emphasis on replacing bans with instruction and student accountability, without specifying a foundational unaided stage. Bliss offers the broadest and most flexible implementation framework: practical critique and simulation exercises, course-specific permissions, protected assessments and equity-sensitive restrictions, including activity-level distinctions between brainstorming, drafting and copying. These contributions are recommendations, reported concerns, survey responses and forecasts rather than proof that staged instruction produces superior durable learning outcomes.

qs.q: For instance, AI might be permitted during an initial brainstorming process when creating an initial outline, but expressly prohibited during drafting and revision.
qs.a: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The 2025 sources collectively build on the proposition by supplying concrete examples of staged or bounded AI integration rather than merely endorsing adoption. The principal implementation logic is that students need practical AI fluency for anticipated legal practice while retaining foundational research, independent analysis and human verification of generated output. CWRU combines general restrictions on AI-assisted drafting with faculty-guided exceptions, while Washington University embeds hands-on AI work within traditional legal-research instruction and trains students to detect inaccurate or fabricated content. Material internal variation remains: the curriculum-focused source directly supports staged use, but the ABA Task Force source establishes only that adoption among responding schools is rapid and uneven and that curricula may become outdated quickly; it does not show whether those schools preserve unaided reasoning or follow staged models. Both sources rely mainly on programme descriptions, survey reporting and educator forecasts, not comparative evidence that these approaches improve durable learning. Because the corpus is curated and the survey figures cover respondents only, this evidence should not be treated as showing how prevalent the staged approach is across legal education.

qs.q: While CWRU Law, like many law schools, has general prohibitions against AI use in drafting assignments, faculty are encouraged to allow exceptions and to guide students in exploring AI’s capabilities responsibly.
qs.a: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: WashU Law is integrating AI as a tool to be used critically and effectively, not as a replacement for human legal reasoning.
qs.a: More Law Schools Embrace AI: Curriculum Integration Across Legal Education · Market & press · 2025

elens.an: The selected 2026 sources collectively build on the proposition that law schools should bridge blanket prohibition and unrestricted adoption through staged, supervised AI use. Their common rationale is that independent legal reasoning remains foundational, but verification and critical supervision of AI are themselves professional competencies that students need to practise before client work. They materially develop the proposition through concrete designs: unaided first-year writing followed by supervised AI-assisted stages; assignment-level permissions tied to learning objectives; oral, handwritten or secure assessments of independent competence; process documentation and oral defence; explicit disclosure, privacy and human-responsibility rules; and periodic policy review. The evidence also adds an important qualification: reported experiments suggest effects vary by task, user, timing and starting ability, while policy archives, pilots and stronger AI-assisted outputs do not establish durable learning gains or the superiority of any curriculum. Material internal variation concerns implementation rather than the dual objective. Chicago and Suffolk most directly operationalise staged integration; commentators favour broader integration across ordinary coursework; Texas states the combined goal without detailed sequencing; the archive and assessment reporting support it descriptively rather than normatively. Berkeley redirects the same goals toward broad default restrictions on assessed work with instructor-authorised exceptions, giving greater priority to protected unaided production. This variation does not make the period mixed overall because even the restrictive approach accepts eventual AI fluency and supervised exceptions. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all law schools or educators, and their number does not indicate the prevalence of any position.
